title: Grow It, Eat It
tagline: Plant science · Responsibility · Food from seed to plate
goal: Your kid plants something they can actually eat, looks after it from seed to plate, and then eats what they grew. That last part does more than it sounds like it should: a radish you pulled out of the dirt yourself tastes different from one in a bag, and a kid who grew it will usually eat it. Along the way they learn that food is grown, not bought, and that living things depend on someone showing up every day.
need: Fast seeds: radishes, lettuce, cress, pea shoots, or basil
A pot, window box or small patch of dirt, and potting soil
Water, a sunny spot, and a notebook for tracking

lesson.text: A plant can't talk, so the skill is reading its signals. Every problem has a symptom you can see, a cause, and a fix.

model.line: The leaves are drooping and the soil is pale and dry.
It hasn't been watered in three days.
Water it slowly until the soil is damp, not soaked.
By the next morning, the leaves are standing up again.

lesson.modelNote: Droopy usually means thirsty, yellow can mean too much water, pale and stretched means it needs more light. Naming the symptom is what makes a fix possible.

howTo.intro: Help with the setup, then hand the plant over and mean it. The temptation is quietly watering it when they forget: a day of droop teaches more than a rescue. Until seedlings have their first true leaves, one quiet reminder is fine.

plan.what: The seed detective game, choose and plant (Steps 1 and 2). 30 minutes.
A daily check, a weekly measurement, and troubleshooting (Steps 3 and 4). 2 minutes a day.
Pick it, cook it, eat it (Step 5).

troubleshoot.a: Let the plant give the feedback: a droop is a better reminder than you. Then help them pick a daily trigger, like right after breakfast.
Often planted too deep or too wet. Check the packet together and try again. It's a useful lesson about following instructions.

troubleshoot.q: The sprouts are tall, pale and flopping
troubleshoot.a: Not enough light, common on a fall or winter windowsill. Move them to your brightest window and turn the pot daily.

steps.title: Be a seed detective
steps.why: A look inside a seed, then choosing what to grow.
steps.kid: Soak a few dried beans or peas in water overnight, then your kid gently splits one open: inside is a tiny baby plant, curled up with its food supply. They lay one soaked bean on a damp paper towel in a clear jar to watch later. Then they pick something edible and fast to grow. Radishes, lettuce, cress and pea shoots are ready in days or a few weeks. They read the seed packet together: how deep, how far apart, how many days to harvest.
steps.you: Let them pick, but nudge toward speed. A six-year-old won't wait two months for a tomato. Radishes are up in about a week and ready in three or four, and that speed is what keeps a kid coming back.
ask: What did you find inside the seed?
How many days does the packet say until harvest?
steps.tip: Read 'days to harvest' on the packet together and pick one that fits your kid's patience, and yours.

levels.explore: Open a soaked bean, then pick cress or pea shoots, the fastest of all.
levels.develop: Draw the inside of the seed, then pick radishes or lettuce.
levels.extend: Work backward from 'days to harvest' so two crops are ready the same week.

steps.title: Plant it and give it a home
steps.why: Your kid plants the seeds themselves and sets up a daily routine.
steps.kid: Your kid fills the pot with soil, pokes holes at the depth the packet says, drops the seeds, covers them and waters gently. Then they choose a sunny spot they walk past every day and pick a daily check-in time: after breakfast, before bed, whenever they'll remember.
steps.you: Help with the first setup, then let their hands do it. Kids plant an inch deep when the packet says a quarter inch. A few that don't come up is its own small lesson. Too deep, a seed can use up its stored food before it reaches light.
ask: How deep and how far apart does the packet say?
Where's the sunniest spot you'll actually walk past every day?
steps.tip: Out of sight is the fastest way for a plant to die. Put it where they'll see it.

levels.explore: Plant a shallow tray of cress on a sunny windowsill.
levels.develop: Plant seeds at the right depth and spacing, and set a daily check-in time.
levels.extend: Sow a few 3 times too deep. Does the seed's stored food last the climb?

steps.title: Keep it alive and track it
steps.why: The daily care, plus a weekly measurement.
steps.kid: Every day your kid checks: is the soil dry, is it getting light, does anything look off? A little water often beats a flood once a week. Once a week, they measure the tallest sprout or sketch the plant and write the date. They notice the plant leaning toward the window and, in the bean jar, the root pushing out before any leaf.
steps.you: Remind once if you must, then let the plant give the feedback. Write the first measurement down with them: the weekly numbers make slow change visible.
ask: How much has it grown since last week?
Which way is it leaning, and why do you think that is?
steps.tip: A simple growth chart (date and height) turns into a real line graph for older kids.

levels.explore: Water it and notice one change a week.
levels.develop: Keep a short daily check and measure it each week.
levels.extend: Chart its height each week, then find the week it grew fastest and what was different.

steps.title: Troubleshoot
steps.why: Something will go a bit wrong, and your kid diagnoses it.
steps.kid: A plant droops, a leaf yellows, the sprouts get leggy and pale. Your kid treats it like a puzzle, the way the example at the start does: what's the symptom, what's the likely cause, what's the fix? Then they check whether it worked.
steps.you: Ask what the plant is telling them before offering answers. A plant that struggles and gets rescued teaches more than one that sails through. For Extend: wet soil with yellow leaves points to too much water, dry crumbly soil to too little.
ask: What does this plant seem to be telling you?
If it's drooping or yellow, what might it need more or less of?
steps.tip: Push a finger into the soil to the first knuckle before watering. Dry there means water, damp means wait.

levels.explore: Notice one thing that looks off.
levels.develop: Guess the cause of a problem and try a fix.
levels.extend: Yellow can mean too much water or too little. How can you tell?

steps.title: Harvest it and eat it
steps.why: The whole point: picking and eating what they grew.
steps.kid: Your kid judges when it's ready (a radish shoulder showing at the soil, lettuce leaves big enough to cut, basil bushy enough to snip) and picks it themselves. Then they eat it: in a salad, on a sandwich, or just rinsed and bitten straight.
steps.you: Help them judge the timing, then make a small moment of the first taste. It might not taste amazing, and that's fine. They grew it and they tried it.
ask: How can you tell it's ready to pick?
Would you grow it again? What would you change?
steps.tip: Even a kid who swears they hate vegetables usually eats the one they grew. Especially that kid.

levels.explore: Pick and taste what you grew.
levels.develop: Judge the right moment, harvest it, and add it to a real meal.
levels.extend: Weigh the harvest, price it at the shop, and see if it paid back the seeds and soil.

conclusion.headline: They ate it.
conclusion.text: Point to a droopy houseplant and watch: they'll push a finger into the soil before saying a word. They know a plant needs checking, not guessing, and that it won't wait for a day they feel like it.
conclusion.celebrate: At the first bite, say: 'Every day you checked on it, and this is what all those mornings made.'
extensions: Plant the next crop straight away, something slower and harder
Give them a real patch of the garden to run
Regrow lettuce or green onions from kitchen scraps
Save seeds from what they grew

signs: They check the plant before you mention it
They notice droops and pale leaves and know what they mean
They try vegetables they grew themselves
makeItReal: Cook a family meal where one ingredient came from their pot, and let them serve it and tell everyone how they grew it, from seed to plate.

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

photo.caption: Spring: the plants go in. Summer: cherry tomatoes, straight into the bowl.

fromHome.text: This spring, my kids decided together what to plant in their small garden. Tomatoes were one of their picks, and the cherry tomatoes worked great: we ate quite a few, straight off the plant.
